```{r load_emergence, include = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
emergence <- read.csv("../../../data/okanagan_sockeye_data/data_clean/fry_emergence.csv")
emergence$yday <- yday(emergence$date)

emergence$time_set_numeric <- with(emergence, {
  hours <- as.numeric(substr(time_set, 1, 2))
  minutes <- as.numeric(substr(time_set, 4, 5)) / 60
  adjusted_hours <- ifelse(hours < 10, hours + 24, hours)  # Add 24 if after midnight
  (adjusted_hours + minutes) - 20
})

emergence <- emergence %>% mutate(volume_m3 = ifelse(volume_m3<0, NA, volume_m3),
                                  mean_nightly_discharge_cms = ifelse(mean_nightly_discharge_cms>100, NA, mean_nightly_discharge_cms)) %>% 
  mutate(total_catch = as.integer(total_catch)) |> 
  filter(sample_year>2002) #2002 was the first year of sampling and methods were not yet worked out



emergence_select <- emergence %>% select(date, brood_year, sample_year, total_catch, soak_time_min, yday, time_set_numeric, volume_m3) %>% 
  mutate(date = as.Date(date)) %>% 
  filter(time_set_numeric >= 0, time_set_numeric<=5) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(total_catch)) |> 
  filter(soak_time_min >=5, soak_time_min<=20)

```


```{r dusk, include = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
dusk <- getSunlightTimes(date = emergence_select$date, lat = 49.1823, lon = -119.5504, keep = "dusk", tz = "Etc/GMT+7")

dusk <- dusk %>% 
  mutate(yday = yday(date)) %>%
  mutate(dusk_hour = hour(dusk) + minute(dusk)/60)

ggplot(dusk, aes(x = yday, y = dusk_hour))+
  geom_point()

emergence_select$dusk <- dusk$dusk_hour

ggplot(emergence_select, aes(x = yday, y = dusk))+
  geom_point()
```

```{r thermal_units, include = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
temperature <- read.csv("../../../data/okanagan_sockeye_data/data_clean/ok_river_mean_daily_temperatures.csv")
#tabyl(temperature, location)
temperature$date <- as.Date(temperature$date)

temperature2 <- read.csv("../../ok_watertemp/data/oliver_air_water_temp_data.csv")
temperature2$date <- as.Date(temperature2$date)

temperature <- temperature %>% 
  select(date, temp = water_temperature_c, location) %>% 
  bind_rows(temperature2 %>% select(date, temp = mean_water_temp) %>% mutate(location = "Oliver2"))

# ggplot(temperature, aes(x = yday(date), y = temp))+
#   geom_line(aes(color = location))+
#   facet_wrap(~year(date))

temp_means <- temperature %>% 
  filter(!(location == "Okanagan River near Oliver, BC" & date >= as.Date("2007-06-01") & date <= as.Date("2008-05-30"))) %>% 
  group_by(date) %>% 
  summarise(temperature = mean(temp,na.rm = TRUE))

ggplot(temp_means, aes(x = yday(date), y = temperature))+
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(100, 319))+
  geom_line()+
  facet_wrap(~year(date))

incubation_start_full <- as.Date("2025-10-15")
incubation_end_full <- as.Date("2025-04-10")

incubation_start <- format(incubation_start_full, "%B ") %>%
  paste0(as.integer(format(incubation_start_full, "%d")))

incubation_end <- format(incubation_end_full, "%B ") %>%
  paste0(as.integer(format(incubation_end_full, "%d")))

ATU.df <- temp_means %>% 
  mutate(yday = yday(date)) |> 
  filter(yday <= 200 | yday > yday(incubation_start_full)) |> 
  mutate(year_start = if_else(format(date, "%m-%d") >= format(incubation_start_full, "%m-%d"),
                              year(date),
                              year(date) - 1)) %>% 
  group_by(year_start) %>% 
  arrange(date, .by_group = TRUE) %>% 
  mutate(ATU = cumsum(temperature)) %>% 
  ungroup()

ggplot(ATU.df, aes(x = yday(date), y = ATU, color = factor(year_start)))+
  geom_path()

ATU_day100 <- ATU.df %>% 
  mutate(yday = yday(date)) %>% 
  mutate(year = year(date)) %>%
  filter(yday == yday(incubation_end_full))

temp_means <- temp_means |> 
  mutate(yday = yday(date)) |> 
  mutate(year = year(date)) |> 
  mutate(incubation = yday < yday(incubation_end_full) | yday > yday(incubation_start_full))
```

```{r moon, include = FALSE}
ATU_emergence_thresh <- 900

new_moons <- data.frame()
for(i in 1:length(unique(emergence$sample_year))){
  year_select <- unique(emergence$sample_year)[i]
  ATU_year <- ATU.df |> filter(year_start == (year_select - 1))
  
  ATU_thresh_date <- ATU_year|> 
    filter(ATU > ATU_emergence_thresh) |> 
    first()
  
  start_date <- ATU_thresh_date$date
  dates <- seq(start_date, start_date+29, by = "day")
  
  new_moon_date = dates[which.min(lunar.illumination(dates))]
  
  new_moons <- bind_rows(new_moons, data.frame(year = year_select, ATU_yday = yday(start_date), new_moon_date = new_moon_date, new_moon_yday = yday(new_moon_date)))
}

env.df <- new_moons %>% 
  left_join(ATU_day100 %>% select(year, ATU))

ggplot(env.df, aes(x = new_moon_yday, y = ATU_yday))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = year))

summary(lm(ATU ~ new_moon_yday, data = env.df))
```

```{r flow, include=FALSE}
flow <- read.csv("../../../data/okanagan_sockeye_data/data_clean/ok_river_mean_daily_flows.csv") %>% 
  mutate(date = as.Date(date), yday = yday(date), year = year(date)) %>% 
  mutate(month_day = format(date, "%m-%d")) %>% 
  group_by(month_day) %>% 
  mutate(life_stage = first(life_stage)) %>% 
  mutate(life_stage2 = ifelse(month_day >= format(incubation_start_full, "%m-%d") | month_day <= format(incubation_end_full, "%m-%d"), "incubation", life_stage)) %>% 
  mutate(life_stage = factor(life_stage, levels = c("incubation", "fry migration", "rearing", "adult migration", "spawn"), ordered = TRUE)) %>% 
  mutate(life_stage2 = factor(life_stage2, levels = c("incubation", "fry migration", "rearing", "adult migration", "spawn"), ordered = TRUE)) %>% 
  ungroup()

flow %>% 
  filter(life_stage2 %in% c("incubation", "fry migration")) %>% 
  filter(brood_year >= min(emergence$brood_year)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = value))+
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(5, 28.3), lty = 2)+
  geom_point(size = 0.1)+
  facet_wrap(~life_stage2)+
  ylab("flow rate m3/s")+
  xlab("")+
  scale_color_discrete(guide = "none")+
  scale_y_log10()

scour_des <- flow %>% 
  filter(life_stage2 %in% c("incubation", "fry migration")) %>% 
  group_by(date) %>% 
  mutate(scour = max(c(value - 28.5, 0)), desiccation = max(c(5 - value, 0))) %>% 
  ungroup()

scour_des_sum <- scour_des %>% 
  group_by(brood_year, life_stage2) %>% 
  summarise(non_range_days = sum(scour > 0) + sum(desiccation>0),
            total_scour = sum(scour), 
            total_desiccation = sum(desiccation), 
            flow_mean = mean(value), 
            flow_max = max(value), 
            flow_min = min(value), 
            flow_median = median(value), n = n()) %>% 
  group_by(life_stage2) %>% 
  mutate(max_n = max(n)) %>% 
  filter(n > max_n-2) %>% 
  select(-n, -max_n) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(year = brood_year + 1)

freshet_mat <- flow %>% 
  filter(year %in% unique(emergence_select$brood_year)) %>% 
  filter(month < c(10)) %>% 
  select(year, yday, value) %>% 
  group_by(yday) %>% 
  mutate(nyears = n()) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  filter(nyears == length(unique(emergence_select$brood_year))) %>% 
  select(-nyears) %>% 
  spread(key = yday, value = value) %>% 
  select(-year) %>% 
  data.matrix()

env.df <- env.df %>% left_join(scour_des_sum %>% filter(life_stage2 == "incubation") %>% select(year, non_range_days, total_scour, total_desiccation))

emergence_select <- left_join(emergence_select |> mutate(date = as.Date(date)), flow |> 
  select(date, daily_flow = value)) |> 
  mutate(volume_m3 = ifelse(volume_m3 == 0, NA, volume_m3))
```

```{r thermal_barrier, include = FALSE}
barrier_thresh <- 22

thermal_barrier <- read.csv("../../Ok_sock_lifecycle_model/outputs/thermal_barrier.csv") %>% 
  select(-X) %>% 
  mutate(fry_year = year + 1) |> 
  mutate(onset_md = format(as.Date(as.Date(onset - 1, origin = "2020-01-01"), origin = "1970-01-01"), "%b %d")) |> 
  filter(threshold == barrier_thresh)

therm_mod <- lm(duration ~ onset, data = thermal_barrier)
thermal_barrier$duration_resid <- thermal_barrier$duration - predict(therm_mod)

ggplot(thermal_barrier |> mutate(onset = as.Date(onset - 1, origin = "2020-01-01")), aes(x = year, y = onset))+
  geom_line()+
  geom_point()+
  labs(x = "", y = "Thermal barrier onset")+

ggplot(thermal_barrier, aes(x = year, y = duration))+
  geom_line()+
  geom_point()+
  labs(x = "", y = "Thermal barrier duration (days)")+
  
  ggplot(thermal_barrier |> mutate(onset = as.Date(onset - 1, origin = "2020-01-01")), aes(x = onset, y = duration))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = year)) +
  labs(x = "Thermal barrier onset",  y = "Thermal barrier duration (days)",)+
  
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")


env.df <- env.df %>% 
  left_join(thermal_barrier |> select(-year), by = c("year" = "fry_year"))

#get air temperatures near Malott for imputation
malott_air <- meteo_pull_monitors(
  monitors = "USW00094197",
  date_min = as.Date(paste(min(env.df$year)-1,06,01,sep = "-"), format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
  date_max = as.Date(paste(max(env.df$year),08,30,sep = "-"), format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
  var = c("TMAX","TMIN")
)

malott_air <- malott_air |> 
  mutate(air_mean = ((tmax + tmin)/2)/10) |> 
  mutate(month = month(date), year = year(date), yday = yday(date))


malott_june_air <- malott_air |> filter(month == 6) |>
  filter(!is.na(air_mean)) |> 
  group_by(year) |> 
  summarise(june_malott_air = mean(air_mean)) |> 
  mutate(fry_year = year+1)

left_join(thermal_barrier, malott_june_air) |> 
ggplot(aes(x = june_malott_air, y = onset - min(onset)+1))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = year))+
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm')+
  scale_y_log10()

env.df <- env.df %>% 
  left_join(malott_june_air |> select(-year), by = c("year" = "fry_year"))
```

```{r stan, include = FALSE}
dayV <- seq(min(emergence_select$yday)-3, max(emergence_select$yday)+5)


dat_list <- list(Y = length(unique(emergence_select$sample_year)),
                 N = nrow(emergence_select),
                 D = length(dayV),
                 year = as.numeric(factor(emergence_select$sample_year)),
                 fry_obs = emergence_select$total_catch,
                 N_missing_volume = sum(is.na(emergence_select$volume_m3)),
                 volume_missidx = which(is.na(emergence_select$volume_m3)),
                 volume = ifelse(!is.na(emergence_select$volume_m3), emergence_select$volume_m3, -999),
                 sample_flow = emergence_select$daily_flow,
                 soak_time = emergence_select$soak_time_min,
                 day = emergence_select$yday - min(emergence_select$yday) + 1,
                 hour = stand(emergence_select$time_set_numeric),
                 new_moon_date = stand(env.df$new_moon_yday),
                 
                 dusk = stand(emergence_select$dusk), 
                 exceeded_FWMT = as.numeric(env.df$non_range_days>0),
                 testalinden = ifelse(env.df$year == 2011, 1, 0),
                 day_std = (dayV - mean(emergence_select$yday))/sd(emergence_select$yday),
                 spawner_ln_est = env.df$spawners_ln_est,
                 spawner_ln_sd = env.df$spawner_ln_sd,
                 
                 N_missing_ATU = sum(is.na(env.df$ATU)),
                 ATU_missidx = which(is.na(env.df$ATU)),
                 ATU = ifelse(!is.na(env.df$ATU), stand(env.df$ATU), -999),
                 
                 N_missing_thermal = sum(is.na(env.df$onset)),
                 thermal_missidx = which(is.na(env.df$onset)),
                 thermal_onset = ifelse(!is.na(env.df$onset), env.df$onset, -999),
                 onset_mean = mean(env.df$onset, na.rm = TRUE),
                 onset_sd = sd(env.df$onset, na.rm = TRUE),
                 onset_low_bound = min(env.df$onset, na.rm = TRUE),
                 
                 thermal_dur_resid = ifelse(!is.na(env.df$duration_resid), env.df$duration_resid/sd(env.df$duration_resid, na.rm = TRUE), -999),
                 
                 malott_june_air = stand(env.df$june_malott_air),
                 
                 freshet_days = ncol(freshet_mat),
                 freshet_flow = freshet_mat,
                 freshet_threshold = 50,
                 freshet_transition_slope = 0.2,

                 sigma_sf_prior = 1,
                 beta_sf_prior = 0,
                 alpha_sf_prior = -3,
                 beta_sf_sigma_prior = 0.5,
                 alpha_sf_sigma_prior = 1
)

init_year <- min(emergence_select$sample_year) - 1

stan_file <- "../code/stan/emergence.stan"
fit <- run_or_load_model(
  model_name = "emerge_m",
  stan_path = stan_file,
  data_list = dat_list, 
  cache_dir = "../model_fits",
  chains = 4, 
  threads_per_chain = 1,
  iter_sampling = 1000,
  iter_warmup = 1000,
  seed = 7, 
  adapt_delta = 0.99
)

```{r fryemerge, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

total_fry_ln <- spread_draws(fit, total_fry_ln[year]) |> 
  mutate(emergence_year = year + init_year) |> 
  mutate(brood_year = emergence_year - 1) |>
  group_by(brood_year, emergence_year) |> 
  summarise(median = median(total_fry_ln), sd = sd(total_fry_ln))

total_fry.df <- spread_draws(fit, total_fry_ln[year]) |> 
  mutate(emergence_year = year + init_year) |> 
  mutate(brood_year = emergence_year - 1) |>
  group_by(brood_year, emergence_year) |> 
  summarise(total_fry = median(exp(total_fry_ln)))

# write.csv(total_fry_ln, 
#           file = "../outputs/fry_est.csv")

env_post <- env.df
env_post <- left_join(env_post, spread_draws(fit, day_peak[year], spawners[year]) |> 
  mutate(day_peak  = day_peak * sd(emergence_select$yday) + mean(emergence_select$yday), 
         year = year + init_year) |> 
  group_by(year) |> 
    summarise(spawners = median(spawners), day_peak = round(median(day_peak))))

env_post <- left_join(env_post, spread_draws(fit, emerging_fry_ln[year, day]) %>% 
                        mutate(year = init_year + year) %>% 
                        group_by(year, day) %>% 
                        summarise(emerge_fry_apex = median(exp(emerging_fry_ln))) %>% 
                        group_by(year) %>% 
                        filter(emerge_fry_apex == max(emerge_fry_apex)) %>% select(-day)) |> 
  mutate(brood_year = year - 1)

p1 <- spread_draws(fit, emerging_fry_ln[year, day]) %>% 
  mutate(brood_year = init_year + year - 1) %>% 
  mutate(date_stnd = day + min(emergence_select$yday) - 1) %>% 
  group_by(brood_year, date_stnd) %>% 
  summarise(fry = median(exp(emerging_fry_ln))) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = date_stnd, y = fry, group = brood_year, color = brood_year))+
  geom_line(size = 1)+
  xlab("")+
  ylab("# of emerging fry (relative)")+
  scale_color_viridis_b(breaks = seq(2002, 2025, by = 4), option = "D", limits = c(2002, 2022), name = "Brood year")+
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 600), expand = c(0, 0))+
  theme(legend.position = c(0.99, 0.99), legend.justification = c(1, 1))+
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "",
    labels = function(y) format(as.Date(y, origin = "2020-01-01"), "%b %d"), expand = c(0, 0)
  )

p2 <- spread_draws(fit, day_peak[year]) %>% 
  mutate(brood_year = init_year + year - 1) %>%
  mutate(day_peak = day_peak * sd(emergence_select$yday) + mean(emergence_select$yday)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = brood_year, y = day_peak))+
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "line")+
  stat_pointinterval()+
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Peak emergence",
    labels = function(y) format(as.Date(y, origin = "2020-01-01"), "%b %d"),
    breaks = seq(92, 126, length = 5)
  )+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = year_breaks)+
  xlab("Brood year")

p3 <- spread_draws(fit, total_fry_ln[year]) |> 
  mutate(brood_year = year + init_year - 1) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = brood_year, y = exp(total_fry_ln)))+
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "line")+
  stat_pointinterval()+
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k"))+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = year_breaks)+
  labs(x = "Brood year", y = "Fry abundance (relative)")

p4 <- spread_draws(fit, day_peak[year]) %>% 
  mutate(year = init_year + year) %>%
  mutate(day_peak = day_peak * sd(emergence_select$yday) + mean(emergence_select$yday)) %>% 
  left_join(env_post |> select(-day_peak)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = new_moon_yday, y = day_peak))+
  # stat_lineribbon(data = moon_emerge.df, aes(x = moon_day, y = day_peak, color = NULL, year = NULL), .width = c(CrIs))+
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, lty = 2)+
  stat_pointinterval(.width = CrIs, aes(color = ATU_yday, group = year))+
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Greys", guide = "none")+
  #geom_text_repel(data = env_post, aes(label = year, y = day_peak_median), color = "dodgerblue2")+
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "B", direction = -1, end = 0.9, 
                        labels = function(y) format(as.Date(y, origin = "2020-01-01"), "%b %d"), "900 ATUs")+
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Estimated peak emergence date",
    labels = function(y) format(as.Date(y, origin = "2020-01-01"), "%b %d")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "First new moon after 900 ATUs",
    labels = function(y) format(as.Date(y, origin = "2020-01-01"), "%b %d")
  )

fig_fry_emerge <- p1 / p2 / p3+

# Abstract

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} salmon; Oncorhynchus; spawner; fry; temperature; flow; incubation; Osoyoos Lake; Okanagan River; Columbia River

\newpage

# Introduction
Sockeye salmon *Oncorhynchus nerka* populations are in decline over much of their southern range in North America [@rand2012; @grant2019], highlighting the urgent need for management measures that can boost survival and contribute to maintenance and recovery. In this context, the Okanagan sockeye represent a rare success story where targeted management measures have proven effective [@alexander2024], resulting in a twentyfold increase in spawner abundance since the early 2000s [@bailey2025]. However, because multiple management measures were implemented concurrently---habitat restoration, a hatchery restocking program, improved dam passage, managing dam outflows to ensure "fish-friendly flows"---and corresponded with changing environmental conditions, it has proven challenging to quantify the contribution of each intervention. Based on a weight of evidence approach, @alexander2024 concluded that these management interventions jointly contributed to the recovery, and amplified the positive effects of a 2007 shift towards more favourable coastal marine conditions. Still, quantitative estimates of how environmental conditions and individual management interventions impact productivity and survival are needed in order to ensure that limited conservation resources are used effectively, and to assess whether similar interventions could support recovery in other salmon populations. 

This study focuses on the spawner-to-fry component of the Okanagan sockeye life cycle, with the goal of understanding how environmental factors and management interventions affect production at this stage. Sockeye spawn in autumn when they lay their eggs in pockets (i.e., redds) in the gravel of streams, and these eggs incubate over the winter, hatching into alevins, before emerging as fry in the spring [@wilson2025]. Productivity during this life stage may be influenced by the number of spawning adults and their condition, the condition of the spawning grounds, and environmental conditions during egg incubation. 

During the incubation period, high flows can scour the stream bed, potentially dislodging or burying eggs and alevins, while also increasing fine sediment infiltration, which in turn reduces oxygen supply [@devries1997; @ingram2011]. Conversely, if flows are low enough to expose the eggs to air, mortality can occur through desiccation or freezing [@casas-mulet2015]. While scouring flows during the incubation period can reduce survival, they may have beneficial effects if they occur at other times of year. Over time, fine sediments can accumulate in spawning habitat, filling the spaces between spawning gravels, and causing mortality by reducing dissolved oxygen and trapping emerging alevins [@moring1982]. High-velocity flows, such as those during freshet, can flush fine sediments from spawning gravel, and may be critical to maintaining productive spawning habitat [@reiser1989].

While desiccation, scour, and sediment flushing occur naturally, they are directly influenced by dam-influenced flow regulation, as is the case in the Okanagan River. Because of this, the Okanagan Basin Implementation Board adopted seasonally varying target flows in 1976, to ensure that flow is suitable for each life stage of salmon in the river [@okanaganbasinimplementationboard1982], but challenges associated with balancing flood mitigation as well as uncertainty in real-time conditions resulted in flows frequently exceeding or falling below this range [@ng2025]. To address this issue, the Fish/Water Management Tool (FWMT) was developed as a decision support tool that provides real-time predictions of the consequences of water management decisions for fish and other users [@hyatt2015]. Since its implementation in 2004, there have been fewer days where flows fell below or exceeded the target flow range [@ng2025; @alexander2024].

It has been assumed that improved flow compliance has reduced scour and desiccation, and thus improved egg to fry survival. However, quantifying this benefit is challenging due to limited fry abundance data prior to FWMT implementation. @ng2025 found that emerging fry recruitment (i.e., fry per spawner) was higher in the 19 years after the FWMT was implemented, compared to the three years prior. Similarly, @alexander2024 found a two-fold increase in the ratio of pre-smolts (i.e., in-lake fry in the fall and winter following emergence) to spawners after brood year 2008 (four years post FWMT implementation) and concluded that FWMT was a strong contributing factor to the sockeye recovery. Despite this, neither study was able to establish a causal link between fry recruitment and interannual variation in flow rates.

Temperatures experienced during the incubation period may influence spawner‑to‑fry production, with embryo survival declining at temperatures of 14-16$^{\circ}$C [@beacham1990; @whitney2013]. However, this range is considerably higher than those observed in the Okanagan River, which rarely exceed 10$^{\circ}$C during incubation. Thus, it remains unclear whether interannual variation in incubation temperatures affects survival of Okanagan sockeye.

Beyond the direct effects of incubation conditions, upstream migration conditions may indirectly influence spawner‑to‑fry production by altering spawner condition, separate from any effects on abundance due to migration mortality. [@fenkes2016]. Elevated river temperatures place considerable stress on migrating sockeye; higher temperatures increase energy use [@rand2006], promote pathogen development [@crossin2008], and reduce aerobic scope [@eliason2011]. This results in reduced migration survival when temperatures exceed 18$^{\circ}$C [@martins2012], particularly for females [@crossin2008; @martins2012a]. There is also evidence that high temperatures encountered during migration lead to egg-retention [@quinn2007], reduced time on the spawning grounds [@minke-martin2018], and reduced egg-to-fry survival [@patterson2004], even when spawners are able to reach the spawning grounds. 

Okanagan sockeye begin their 830 km migration up the mainsteam of the Columbia River in mid June, passing by nine hydroelectric dams and reaching the confluence of the Okanagan River (spelled Okanogan in the U.S.A.) by late June or early July. From there, they migrate an additional 185 km up the Okanagan River reaching their spawning grounds above Osoyoos Lake. Summer temperatures in the lower Okanagan River routinely thermal barrier to migration, forcing fish to hold in Lake Pateros at the confluence with the Columbia River and resulting in considerable thermal stress [@miller-saunders2024] and en-route mortality [@hyatt2020]. Observations of broodstock collected by the Okanagan Nation Alliance `r paste0("kł c", "p", "\u0313", "\u0259", "l", "k", "\u0313", " stim", "\u0313")` hatchery indicate that fish that were forced to hold in Lake Pateros for an extended period produced fewer eggs compared to fish that were transported past the thermal barrier and held in cooler hatchery waters (pers. comm. D. Stefanovic and T. Marsel), despite documented negative effects of maternal hatchery holding on egg size [@sopinka2016]. It is therefore plausible that the timing and duration of the thermal barrier may impact the productivity of the fish that survive to reach the spawning grounds. 

Here we present a process-based Bayesian model that estimates how flow velocity and temperature, during and preceding the incubation period, influence spawner-to-fry production of sockeye salmon in the Okanagan River. This model allows us to test the following hypotheses: (1) higher pre-spawning flows increase production by flushing fine sediments from spawning gravel; (2) production is reduced in years when incubation-period flows fall outside the FWMT target range ($5\text{–}28.5~\mathrm{m}^3/\mathrm{s}$), reflecting increased scour and desiccation risk; (3) interannual variation in incubation temperature has limited effects on production because temperatures during incubation generally remain within ranges suitable for embryo survival; (4) production is reduced in years when the thermal barrier in the lower Okanagan forms earlier and lasts longer, through carry-over effects of thermal stress on spawner condition. By quantifying the benefits of flow management for salmon and the risks posed by warming temperatures, this work supports the continued application of the Fish/Water Management Tool and provides insight into how similar approaches may support the sustainable management of Okanagan sockeye and other salmon populations.


# Methods 
## Study system
### Salmon enumeration
### Spawners
Spawner abundance was estimated using a previously published Bayesian model fit to spawner enumeration surveys conducted by the Okanagan Nation Alliance (ONA) in the Okanagan River Index section between Osoyoos and Vaseux lakes [Figure \ref{fig:map}\; @thompsoninreview]. That model accounts for observation error and repeated counts of individuals on the spawning grounds producing annual posterior distributions of total spawner abundance. For the present analysis, we used the posterior mean and standard deviation of log spawner abundance as inputs to the spawner-to-fry recruitment model (described subsequently), thereby propagating uncertainty from the spawner estimation process.

### Fry emergence
The ONA has conducted fry emergence surveys in the Okanagan River each spring (March–May) since `r min(emergence_select$sample_year)`; trial sampling in 2002 was excluded because methods were not standardized. Sampling occurs approximately weekly early in the emergence period and increases to every 3–4 days during peak emergence, with reduced frequency thereafter.

Emerging fry are sampled at Vertical Drop Structure 13 (Figure \ref{fig:map}) using a fyke net (1 $\times$ 2 ft opening; 5 mm stretch mesh) with typically four sets per night, each with a target soak time of 15 minutes. For each set, total fry catch, soak time, and set start time are recorded. Since 2008, a flow meter has been used to estimate the sampled water volume for each set. To reduce heterogeneity in sampling conditions (particularly in early years), our analysis only includes sets conducted between 20:00 and 01:00 with soak times between 5 and 20 minutes.  

## Environmental covariates
### Upstream migration thermal barrier
We define the thermal barrier period as the days between June 25 and September 30 where minimum daily water temperatures in the lower Okanagan River, measured in Malott Washington, exceed `r barrier_thresh` $^{\circ}$C without a break of at least five days. Although river temperatures can exceed `r barrier_thresh` $^{\circ}$C before June 25th, we set this as the earliest barrier date because no more than 5% of the run has passed Wells dam (directly downstream) in the past 25 years [@columbiariverdartcolumbiabasinresearchuniversityofwashington2025].

The onset date of the thermal barrier is the first day of this period and the duration is the number of days that the thermal barrier lasts. In years where water temperatures never exceed `r barrier_thresh` $^{\circ}$C, we define the onset date as 10 days after the latest onset date observed in the dataset. This allowed us to have a continuous covariate scale for our models, rather than leaving onset date in these years as undefined. Duration is strongly negatively correlated with onset date (*r* = `r round(cor(thermal_barrier$onset, thermal_barrier$duration), 2)`), reflecting the fact that duration is likely to be longer when onset is early. To separate these effects, we used residual duration, from a linear model of duration as a function of onset date, which represents whether the barrier lasted longer or shorter than expected for its onset.

Because water temperatures at Malott are not available prior to `r min(thermal_barrier$year)`, we treated thermal-barrier onset and residual duration as partially missing covariates and estimated them within the Bayesian spawner-to-fry recruitment model. For years with missing Malott temperature data, standardized onset date (mean = 0, sd = 1) was modelled as a linear function of mean June air temperature from the nearby NOAA station USW00094197, with residual error estimated from the years with observed onset. Residual duration (scaled by its standard deviation) was treated as partially missing and estimated within the Bayesian model by assuming a skew-normal distribution across years; missing values were inferred under this distribution.


### Incubation period flow and temperature
We define the incubation period as `r incubation_start` to `r incubation_end`. These dates are defined based on when spawners are most abundant on the spawning grounds and just prior to when emerging fry are most abundant in the emergence samples [@stockwell2020]. To estimate flow rates on the spawning grounds, we use daily flow rates in the Okanagan River near Oliver, which is monitored by the Water Survey of Canada (Station 08NM085). This station is directly downstream of the spawning grounds where spawner enumeration and fry emergence sampling occurs (Figure \ref{fig:map}). In each year, we calculate: 1) whether any incubation-day discharge fell outside the FWMT target range of $5\text{–}28.5~\mathrm{m}^3/\mathrm{s}$, 2) the accumulated thermal units (ATUs) at the end of the incubation period (i.e., `r incubation_end`). ATUs were calculated as the cumulative sum of mean daily water temperatures over the incubation period for each brood year. 

### Pre-spawn flushing flows
We characterized pre‑spawn flushing conditions using daily discharge from the Okanagan River near Oliver (Water Survey of Canada station 08NM085) during January–September prior to each spawning season (Figure X). To summarize the extent to which flows were capable of mobilizing fine sediments within the spawning gravel, we constructed an annual flushing index:

$$\text{flush}_y = \sum_{d \in D_y}\text{logit}^{-1}(k_{\text{flush}} \cdot (Q_{y,d} - Q^*))$$

where $Q_{y,d}$ is the discharge on day $d$ in year $y$ and $D_y$ includes all days from January through September. The parameters $Q^*$ and $k_{\text{flush}}$ define how daily discharge is translated into a flushing intensity between 0 and 1. Summing across days allows the flushing effects to accumulate over the year preceding spawning.

We selected values for these parameters based on observations of gravel mobility in the Okanagan River spawning grounds, which show that movement begins to occur at around 28 $\mathrm{m}^3/\mathrm{s}$ (aligned with the FWMT upper threshold for incubation flows), with full movement occurring at around 70 $\mathrm{m}^3/\mathrm{s}$ [@summitenvironmentalconsultantsltd.2002]. Thus, we set $Q^*$ at the discharge corresponding to the approximate midpoint of this transition (`r dat_list$freshet_threshold` $\mathrm{m}^3/\mathrm{s}$), and $k_{\text{flush}}$ to produce a smooth logistic response spanning the observed range of gravel movement. 

```{r envfig, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=7, fig.pos='center',fig.cap = "Annual environmental covariates used in the spawner-to-fry production model. (A) Date of the thermal barrier onset in the lower Okanagan River. (B) Linear relationship between thermal barrier onset date and duration (days) used to derive duration residuals. (C) Residual barrier duration (days), after accounting for onset timing. (D) Pre-spawn flushing index. (E) Binary indicator of whether the FWMT range was maintained during incubation. (F) Accumulated thermal units (ATU) during incubation. Environmental data are shown corresponding to the brood year that would be impacted. Lines show observed values or posterior medians in years with imputed data. Intervals (66% and 95%) are shown only for imputed values."}
spread_draws(fit, thermal_onset_merge[y]) |> 
  mutate(year = y + init_year - 1) |> 
ggplot(aes(x = year, y = thermal_onset_merge))+
  stat_pointinterval(pch = NA)+
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "line")+
  labs(x = "Brood year", y = "Thermal barrier onset")+
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = function(d) format(as.Date(d - 1, origin = "2020-01-01"), "%b %d"),
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 5),
  )+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = year_breaks)+

ggplot(env.df, aes(x = onset, y = duration))+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black")+
  geom_point()+
    scale_x_continuous(
    labels = function(d) format(as.Date(d - 1, origin = "2020-01-01"), "%b %d"),
    breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 3),
  )+
  labs(x = "Barrier onset", y = "Barrier duration (days)")+

  spread_draws(fit, thermal_dur_resid_merge[y]) |> 
  mutate(year = y + init_year - 1) |> 
  mutate(dur_resid = thermal_dur_resid_merge * sd(env.df$duration_resid, na.rm = TRUE) + mean(env.df$duration_resid, na.rm = TRUE)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = dur_resid))+
  stat_pointinterval(pch = NA)+
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "line")+
  labs(x = "Brood year", y = "Barrier duration (resid. days)")+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = year_breaks)+

  spread_draws(fit, fresh_days[y]) |> 
  mutate(year = y + init_year - 1) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = fresh_days))+
  stat_pointinterval(pch = NA)+
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "line")+
  labs(x = "Brood year", y = "Pre-spawn flushing index")+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = year_breaks)+

  ggplot(env.df, aes(x = brood_year, y = as.numeric(non_range_days == 0))) +
  geom_line()+
  #geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1), labels = c("No", "Yes"), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Brood year", y = "FWMT range maintained")+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = year_breaks)+

  ggplot(env.df, aes(x = brood_year, y = ATU))+
  geom_line()+
  labs(x = "Brood year", y = "Incubation ATUs")+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = year_breaks)+
  
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")+
  plot_layout(ncol = 2)

```

## Directed acyclic graph and overall model structure
The assumed causal pathways and observation structure are summarized in a directed acyclic graph (DAG\; Figure \ref{fig:DAG}), which separates (1) annual spawner‑to‑fry production, (2) within‑year emergence phenology linking annual fry abundance to daily emergence intensity, and (3) the observation process linking daily emergence to set‑level catches via sampling effort and timing. The DAG guided the structure of our joint Bayesian model, which we describe in the subsequent sections. The model combines multiple submodels in a single joint likelihood implemented in Stan [@stan2024] and fit in R version getRversion() [@rcoreteam2024] using cmdstanr [@gabry2024].

```{r DAG, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=12, fig.height=8, fig.pos='center',fig.cap = "Directed acyclic graph (DAG) showing model structure linking spawner abundance, environmental drivers, fry emergence phenology, and observed set-level fry catches. Node colours indicate: latent/process variables (purple), environmental drivers (blue), sampling/observation variables (grey), and the observed response (red). NOTE: this is a placeholder until I can produce a nicer looking DAG."}

## Estimating a metric of yearly fry abundance
The goal of these surveys is to estimate the peak and end dates of emergence. However, they can also provide a relative index of total fry abundance in each year $\hat{N}_y^{\text{fry}}$. The index is relative because the proportion of all emerging fry that are sampled is unknown. This annual index of fry abundance is treated as a latent state representing the relative seasonal total of emerging fry. It is shared by both the emergence observation submodel and the spawner-to-fry recruitment submodel within a joint likelihood, as outlined in the subsequent sections. The emergence data inform $\hat{N}_y^{\text{fry}}$, while the recruitment submodel provides its expectation as a function of spawner abundance and environmental covariates.

### Fry-emergence submodel
To specify the latent emergence process, we assume that fry emerge over a range of days that is approximated by a normal distribution. Additionally, emergence is assumed to vary in intensity across the day, peaking in the evening, again approximating a normal distribution. This is intended as a phenomenological approximation of emergence patterns, rather than as a mechanistic model of individual emergence timing. The total number of fry, as well as the seasonal timing and spread of their emergence, vary across years such that:

$$\hat{N}_{y,d}^{\text{fry}} = \frac{\hat{N}_y^{\text{fry}}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\ d_y^{\text{sd}}\ \sqrt{2\pi} h^{\text{sd}}} \cdot 
\exp\!\left(-\frac{(d - d_y^{\text{peak}})^2}{2(d_y^{\text{sd}})^2} \right),$$


where $\hat{N}_{y,d}^{\text{fry}}$ is the expected emergence intensity on day $d$ in year $y$, evaluated at the peak hour $h^{\text{peak}}$. This equation ensures that the implied emergence integrates to $\hat{N}_y^{\text{fry}}$ across days and hours in the year. The parameters $d_y^{\text{peak}}$ and $d_y^{\text{sd}}$ represent the peak timing and spread of emergence across days in year $y$, modelled hierarchically across years (peak on the linear scale; spread on the log scale). The parameter $h^{\text{sd}}$ is the spread of emergence in a day, which we assume is constant across days and years. We used standardized (mean = 0, sd = 1) day $d$ and hour $h$ in the model. The within-day peak timing parameter $h^{\text{peak}}$ does not appear in this expression because $\hat{N}_{y,d}^{\text{fry}}$ represents the emergence intensity evaluated at that peak hour; the hourly distribution around that peak is incorporated in the observation model (outlined below).

We linked the latent emergence intensity to the observed fry counts from the individual sets using a negative binomial likelihood with an overdispersion parameter $\phi^{\text{fry}}$. Thus, the expected fry count for set $i$ depends on the emergence intensity on day $d_i$ in year $y_i$, adjusting for volume sampled, and the standardized set hour $h_i$:

\begin{align*}
N_i^{\text{fry}_{\text{obs}}} &\sim \text{NegativeBinomial}(\mu^{\text{fry}}_i, \phi^{\text{fry}}) \\
\mu^{\text{fry}}_i &= \exp\left( \log \hat{N}_{y_i, d_i}^{\text{fry}} + \beta^{\text{volume}} \cdot (\log(\text{volume}_i) - \log(100)) - \frac{(h_i - h^{\text{peak}})^2}{2 (h^{\text{sd}})^2} \right), \\
\end{align*}

where $\beta^{\text{volume}}$ is the rate at which fry abundance increases with sampled volume $\text{volume}_i$, expressed relative to 100 m$^3$. The parameter $h^{\text{peak}}$ is the hour of peak emergence in the day, and $h^{\text{sd}}$ is the spread of emergence across hours in a day. 

Missing sampled volume was imputed jointly within the full Bayesian model using a lognormal regression of sampled volume on soak time and daily flow (both log-transformed). The parameters were estimated based on the observed volumes and missing values were imputed based on these relationships. 


### Spawner-to-fry recruitment submodel  
We modelled expected fry abundance $\mu_y^{\text{sf}}$ in year $y$ as a Shepherd function [@shepherd1982] of spawner abundance $N_y^{\text{spawners}}$:

$$\mu_y^{\text{sf}} = \frac{\alpha_y^{\text{sf}} \cdot p_y^{\text{eff}} \cdot N_y^{\text{spawners}}}{1 + (\beta_y^{\text{sf}} \cdot N_y^{\text{spawners}}/10^5)^{\theta^{\text{sf}}}},$$
where $\alpha_y^{\text{sf}}$ is the density-independent production rate in year $y$, $\beta_y^{\text{sf}}$ is the rate of density dependence, and $\theta^{\text{sf}}$ governs the shape of density dependence. $p_y^{\text{eff}}$ is a proportional scaling factor that reduces the effective reproductive contribution of each spawner, based on thermal conditions experienced during upstream migration (see below). This spawner-to-fry recruitment function reduces to the Beverton-Holt [@beverton1957] form when $\theta^{\text{sf}}=1$ and approaches a Ricker [@ricker1954] form when $\theta^{\text{sf}}\to\infty$. Thus, it is a generalized version, which does not assume any specific functional form for density dependence. We divide $N_y^{\text{spawners}}$ by $10^5$ in the denominator to keep $\beta_y^{\text{sf}}$ near one, avoiding the need for very small parameter values.

### Density-independent productivity during incubation
We allow the density-independent production rate $\alpha_y^{\text{sf}}$ to vary from year-to-year based on environmental conditions experienced during incubation, modelling it as a log-linear function in order to ensure positivity:

$$\log \alpha_y^{\text{sf}} = \alpha_0^{\text{sf}} + \beta^{\text{FWMT}} \cdot \text{FWMT}_y + \beta^{\text{ATU}} \cdot \text{ATU}_y.$$
The parameter $\alpha_0^{\text{sf}}$ is the density-independent production rate in average conditions and the $\beta$ coefficients are the slope parameters that estimate the effect of whether or not discharge exceeded the FWMT target range at any point during the incubation period ($\beta^{\text{FWMT}}$) and accumulated thermal units during incubation ($\beta^{\text{ATU}}$).

### Thermal barrier impacts on per-capita spawner effectiveness
We model the effect of upstream migration thermal conditions on spawner-to-fry production as a reduction in per-capita spawner reproductive effectiveness. We use a logistic function to represent this effect, reflecting the assumption that delayed thermal-barrier onset can increase effectiveness only up to the point at which all returning salmon have successfully migrated, beyond which additional delays confer no further benefit:

$$p_y^{\text{eff}} = \text{logit}^{-1}(\alpha_0^{\text{eff}} +\beta^{\text{onset}} \cdot \text{onset}_y + \beta^{\text{dur}} \cdot \text{dur}_y),$$ 
where $\alpha_0^{\text{eff}}$ represents baseline per-capita spawner effectiveness on the logit scale under average conditions, $\beta^{\text{onset}}$ describes the effect of thermal-barrier onset date, and $\beta^{\text{dur}}$ is the additional effect of barrier duration beyond that explained by onset timing. We parameterized this logistic relationship using a transition-width parameter that controls how rapidly spawner effectiveness changes across years. The onset and residual-duration slope coefficients were scaled by this transition width. 

### Density dependence and pre-spawn flushing
We assume that density dependence during spawner-to-fry recruitment occurs primarily through crowding on the spawning grounds. As spawner abundance increases, there is greater competition for suitable spawning sites. This pushes spawners into suboptimal gravel and can lead to superimposition, whereby later-arriving spawners build their redds on top of those built by earlier-arriving fish, reducing egg survival through disturbance and displacement [@burgner1969; @essington2000]. Thus, we assume that the effects of pre-spawn flushing of fine sediments should impact the population by changing the amount and quality of available spawning gravel [@moring1982; @reiser1989]. 

We modelled annual variation in density dependence as a function of the flushing index defined above. Specifically, we allowed the density-dependence parameter to vary log-linearly with the standardized flushing index:
$$\log \beta_y^{\text{sf}} = \beta_0^{\text{sf}} + \beta^{\text{flush}} \cdot \left(\frac{\text{flush}_y}{\operatorname{sd}(\text{flush})}\right).$$


### Process error and spawner uncertainty
We assume that the annual fry abundance index $\hat{N}_y^{\text{fry}}$ deviates from its expected value $\mu_y^{\text{sf}}$ due to process error $\sigma_{\text{proc}}^{\text{sf}}$, with log abundance following a normal distribution around the expected value:

$$\log \hat{N}_y^{\text{fry}} \sim \text{Normal}(\log \mu_y^{\text{sf}}, \sigma_{\text{proc}}^{\text{sf}}).$$
To propagate uncertainty in spawner abundance, we model log spawner abundance $\log N_y^{\text{spawners}}$ as a latent variable:

$$\log N_y^{\text{spawners}} \sim \text{Normal}(\hat{\mu}_y^{\text{spawners}}, \hat{\sigma}_y^{\text{spawners}})$$

where $\hat{\mu}_y^{\text{spawners}}$ and $\hat{\sigma}_y^{\text{spawners}}$ are the mean and standard deviation of log spawner abundance from @thompsoninreview. Full prior specifications are provided in Table \ref{tab:priorstable}.

## Quantifying environmental impacts on spawner-to-fry production
We estimated scenario-based contrasts in predicted fry production by varying each environmental covariate while holding all others at their mean value. Except when estimating its effect, the FWMT incubation flow rate range was assumed to be maintained. Predictions were generated at the median observed spawner abundance over the study period. For each contrast, fry production was estimated with the focal variable set to the `r low*100`% (low or short) and `r high*100`% (high or long) quantiles of its observed distribution. For the FWMT effect, we compared scenarios where incubation flows were maintained within the FWMT range (i.e., $\text{FWMT}_y = 0$) throughout the incubation period and where the flow exceeded this range at least once during incubation (i.e., $\text{FWMT}_y = 1$). For each posterior draw, we calculated the percent difference between scenarios. Percent change was calculated using the scenario with higher median predicted fry production as the reference state, such that all estimates are expressed as reductions in spawner-to-fry production.

# Results
We estimate that when the thermal barrier begins early (`r format(as.Date(as.Date(quantile(thermal_barrier$onset, low) - 1, origin = "2020-01-01"), origin = "1970-01-01"), "%B %d")`), fry production production declines by approximately
`r -round(median(fry_percent_change$onset))`% compared with a late onset (`r format(as.Date(as.Date(quantile(thermal_barrier$onset, high) - 1, origin = "2020-01-01"), origin = "1970-01-01"), "%B %d")`)(95\% CrI: `r -round(quantile(fry_percent_change$onset,0.975))`\% to `r -round(quantile(fry_percent_change$onset,0.025))`\%). 

The impact of long versus short thermal barrier duration, independent of onset date, is estimated to reduce fry production by `r -round(median(fry_percent_change$dur))`%, with a `r round(mean(fry_percent_change$dur<0) * 100)`% probability that the effect is negative (95\% CrI: `r -round(quantile(fry_percent_change$dur,0.975))`\% to `r -round(quantile(fry_percent_change$dur,0.025))`\%). 

In years with low pre-spawn flushing, fry production is estimated to be `r -round(median(fry_percent_change$freshet))`% lower compared to what it would be in years with high pre-spawn flushing, with a `r round(mean(fry_percent_change$freshet<0) * 100)`% probability that the effect is negative (95\% CrI: `r -round(quantile(fry_percent_change$freshet,0.975))`\% to `r -round(quantile(fry_percent_change$freshet,0.025))`\%). 

Allowing flows during the incubation period to exceed the target range from the Fish Water Management Tools $(5\text{ – }28.5~\mathrm{m}^3/\mathrm{s})$ is estimated to decrease fry production by `r -round(median(fry_percent_change$FWMT))`% (95\% CrI: `r -round(quantile(fry_percent_change$FWMT,0.975))`\% to `r -round(quantile(fry_percent_change$FWMT,0.025))`\%).

In years with low incubation accumulated thermal units, fry production is estimated to be `r -round(median(fry_percent_change$ATU))`% lower compared to what it would be in years with high incubation accumulated thermal units, with a `r round(mean(fry_percent_change$ATU<0) * 100)`% probability that the effect is negative (95\% CrI: `r -round(quantile(fry_percent_change$ATU,0.975))`\% to `r -round(quantile(fry_percent_change$ATU,0.025))`\%).
